Photograph: Eunavfor Aspides Handout/EPA First Edition newsletter Yemen Thursday briefing: Yemen’s war continues to threaten oil supplies– but what about its people? In today’s newsletter: The Houthi advance along the Red Sea coast raised fears for global trade and energy supplies, while more than 100,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the fighting Libby Brooks Thu 17 Sep 2026 01.45 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 01.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. The lightning advance of Houthi militants along the west coast of Yemen over the past week has prompted fears of a spiralling conflict in the region and a new oil supply crisis. For families living in the Middle East’s poorest country, the most significant fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces in years is a crisis upon a catastrophe, with escalating civilian casualties and at least 100,000 displaced in recent days. Houthi fighters have captured strategic islands across a critical Red Sea trade route, the Bab al-Mandab strait, one of the most important shipping routes in the world – almost 15% of global sea trade passes through it. The strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil and gas transited in peacetime, has remained largely blocked since the US and Israel launched airstrikes in February, so the prospect of Iran and its allies exerting pressure on two maritime choke points has global implications. The price of crude oil has already begun to spike . For today’s newsletter, I spoke to Farea Al-Muslimi , a research fellow at Chatham House, about this new and dangerous dimension to the ongoing war in Yemen, and why fears over oil and global trade must not overshadow the plight of ordinary Yemenis. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Key allies of Andy Burnham have warned the prime minister not to back down over his promises to put water companies under public control, after details emerged about the prime minister’s plan to give mayors more oversight of the industry. Environment | Climate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal and Tibet last month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found. Health | Women with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found . Europe | The UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said. UK news | Police searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex border have found a body . In depth: The fight for Yemen’s Red Sea coast View image in fullscreen Yemen refugees arrive in Djibouti as intensified fighting drives displacement. Photograph: International Organization for Migration/Reuters The current escalation of violence in Yemen has its roots in a civil war that broke out in 2014 between the Yemeni army and the Houthi movement, which champions Yemen’s Shia Muslim minority. A year later, the Houthis – part of Iran’s “axis of resistance”, a loose coalition of armed groups that includes Hamas and Hezbollah – toppled the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. Al-Muslimi grew up in a remote mountain village in Yemen, where his family made honey, one of the country’s most lucrative and popular exports. His mother used to tease him because the bees didn’t recognise him after he spent long periods studying away from home – he was the only person in his family who had to wear a beekeeping suit. Al-Muslimi now writes about how the years-long internecine conflict has had a devastating impact on the honey trade and the farmers who tend Yemeni bees. At least 150,000 people have been killed since 2014, mainly through aerial bombardment by the Saudi-backed coalition that supports the Yemeni government, which has resumed this week. About 4.5 million people – the population of Birmingham and Greater Manchester combined – have already been displaced by fighting over the past decade, while the UN estimates that more than 18.2 million – twice the population of London – are in dire need of humanitarian assistance. The situation now is “worse than 2015”, says Al-Muslimi, with global attention diverted to crises in Syria, Sudan, and Ukraine and now focused on oil prices and regional consequences. “There is even less willingness to help civilians.” After the Houthis captured the port city of Mocha, birthplace of the global coffee trade, last week, Al-Muslimi heard local media reports of more than 240 pregnant women ready to give birth without accessible healthcare. “It’s absolutely nuts,” he says. “This is a country that was already suffering so many things, including indifference.” How has the conflict escalated in the past week? It has been plain for months to Yemen-watchers that the Houthis were preparing for a significant offensive, says al-Muslimi. This erupted about a week ago with the militants seizing control of parts of the west coast and gaining a hold over the Bab al-Mandab strait, including the strategic port of Mocha and key islands of Perim, Greater and Lesser Hanish in the 20-mile stretch of water that forms a natural chokepoint on the trade route connecting Asia with Europe. With government supporters in disarray, the degree of division among anti-Houthi forces is complicating the fight back. The Houthis have achieved what Al-Muslimi calls “the most consequential change in territorial control in Yemen for years”. Since then, the Houthis have claimed responsibility for missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, including the bombing of a critical east-west oil pipeline. On Wednesday a military spokesperson for the Houthis denied attempting to fly a drone close to the holy city of Mecca, and claimed that Saudi Arabia has carried out as many as 450 airstrikes in Yemen ‌this week in retaliation. The ongoing aggression is driving fears that more Muslim nations could be drawn into the conflict. What does it mean for global oil supply? If ​the Houthis were to close the Bab al-Mandab strait, vessels would be forced to reroute all the way around the southern tip of Africa. The consequences for the global economy could be dire, particularly when taken along with the ongoing blockade of Hormuz. With Iran and its Houthi allies controlling potentially a third of energy trade globally, “it’s more dangerous than a nuclear bomb,” says Al-Muslimi bluntly, “especially at a time when the world still depends massively on this type of energy”. Attacks on Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline – which is now closed for repairs and has been crucial for moving oil from the strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea export hub of Yanbu – will add further pressure to global supplies. Al-Muslimi advises caution over Houthi claims that they don’t intend to impose transit fees on vessels passing through Bab al-Mandab. The UN security council has seen evidence that, since the militants started attacks on Red Sea shipping in 2023, in response to Israel’s decimation of Gaza, the Houthis have been extracting informal payments from some shipping agencies in return for safe passage. Meanwhile, Saudi anger with Iran for assisting Houthi attacks saw the cancellation of a meeting with Gulf states about the future of the strait of Hormuz on Monday. Reports in the early hours today that Saudi Arabia may be offering more crude cargoes through Oman saw the price of Brent crude drop to $104.59 a barrel after hitting $108 earlier this week. But for perspective, it was trading at $80 a barrel in early July. This comes as the average price of diesel in the US hit $6 per gallon for the first time last week, with the Iran war, combined with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, continuing to squeeze supply. What does it mean for the region? The UN security council held an emergency meeting in New York on Tuesday to discuss the escalating violence in Yemen and threats to maritime security, with members urging maximum restraint to avoid the situation devolving into a wider regional war. The conflict is the first test of a mutual defence pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, announced in August – but Saudi has yet to publicly call on either for assistance. Meanwhile, Al-Muslimi says the US, a close Saudi ally, faces a dilemma. The States reached a truce with the Houthis in May 2025, after conducting airstrikes against the group after attacks on Red Sea shipping. “The existing truce gives both sides reasons for restraint,” he says. “For Trump, preserving that arrangement helps keep the US away from another costly Middle Eastern military confrontation while it remains engaged in the strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have equally strong incentives to not be drawn into conflict with the US, which caused them serious damage in the 2025 bombing campaign.” Yesterday the Guardian confirmed that officials from the US had met Houthi leaders over the weekend in Oman, where they received assurances that the ceasefire still held and that the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. While Trump condemned the Houthi advance for threatening freedom of navigation, he has far rejected any military response in support of Riyadh. Al-Muslimi calls for a more coherent international approach to his country, which he considers one of the least understood in the region. Yemen analysts have frequently criticised the US and allies for approaching Yemen’s challenges with a focus on security rather than diplomacy or development, while internal instability has been exploited by larger regional powers to fight their own proxy battles. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “Prisoners to ‘double up’ in single prefab jail cell units”, is the Guardian ’s front page today. The Mail splashes on “‘Rest assured, we will forget her soon enough’”, the Times has “King: Grief has coloured earl’s claims over Diana”, the Telegraph writes “Palace hits back at Diana’s brother”, and the Sun ’s take is “Recollections may vary … again”. The Mirror ’s front page is “Heartbreak”, the i Paper ’s splash is “Burnham warns of ‘challenging’ budget after 3.1% inflation”, and the Express says “We are ‘paying the price’ for Labour’s economy failure”. The FT leads on “Fed raises rates despite Trump pressure in bid to tame prices”. Lastly, Metro runs with “‘Putney pusher’ suspect dead”. Today in Focus: The Latest Photograph: The Guardian Ed Sheeran support acts quit after Macklemore ‘Free Palestine’ row All four supporting acts for the upcoming dates of Ed Sheeran’s tour have withdrawn in solidarity with fellow opener Macklemore. The American rapper was removed from Sheeran’s tour after comments made onstage in support of Palestine. Sheeran responded that venue owners – including Robert Kraft who owns the New England Patriots and its home stadium – had objected to Macklemore’s appearance on the tour. But after he had tried to negotiate with the venue owners ‘at length to build bridges’, ultimately the promoters made the decision to pull the plug. Artists who have pulled out include Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Beoga. Lucy Hough speaks to Guardian assistant opinion editor Jason Okundaye. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-energ.text: DUBLIN — European energy officials highlighted handouts and tax cuts as among the few viable ways to shield consumers from surging energy costs this winter — while hoping that U.S. President Donald Trump wouldn't add fuel to the fire by banning American diesel exports. At an informal gathering in Dublin Tuesday, European energy ministers faced a grim reality. Natural gas prices are at near four-year highs ahead of winter, European gas reserves are unusually low, and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East means the Strait of Hormuz remains shut indefinitely. Meanwhile, soaring diesel costs have prompted the U.S. to consider banning exports of the motor fuel, which would disproportionately affect Europe. Ministers and EU officials said that harnessing Europe's potential for renewables with deep upgrades to its grid and electricity markets was the only real way to bring down costs in the long-term. But in the short term, they talked up the benefits of financial support schemes to boost electrification and renewables uptake — many of which were already adopted in the wake of the first energy crisis this year. Advertisement Advertisement "We see more EVs than ever sold in Europe now, we see electric heat pumps replacing gas boilers and oil boilers than ever before — so yes, there are actually a lot of positive things happening," EU energy chief Dan Jørgensen told reporters in a response to a question from POLITICO. "Many times, one of the best things we can do in these situations that also works in the short term is active electrification." He added that he was "in no way implying that that is enough," and there were "many big structural things that we need to do that will not help consumers tomorrow or even this year, but there are actually also things that member states can do." Irish Energy Minister Darragh O'Brien, whose government holds the EU's six-month rotating presidency, also described the deployment of renewables as the main way to address rising costs, emphasizing that Dublin was working to hasten the adoption of a new EU law aimed at strengthening the bloc's electricity grids. But he said the EU's ability to address the current rise in costs was limited. "There are flexibilities that member states have at our disposal around taxation, but I think our citizens are aware that there's no government in Europe that is going to be able to protect their citizens from every single price increase," he told reporters. "The fundamental reason for that," he said, was "our over-dependence in the European Union on imported fossil fuel." Discussions were dominated by the question of where responsibility for addressing rising prices ought to lie. Member countries called on the Commission to institute a windfall tax on energy companies making bumper profits, while the EU executive said it was up to individual countries to decide. Advertisement Advertisement The same went for a call by Jørgensen last week for consumers to reduce fuel use; national capitals would rather wait for central guidance from the Commission, according to a European energy official familiar with member-country deliberations who, like others cited in this piece, was granted anonymity to speak openly. Both O'Brien and Jørgensen also warned that it was important for such measures to be targeted and temporary to avoid uneven application that could distort the EU's single market. The despair over energy costs lent an experimental air to the closed-door discussions held in the imposing Dublin Castle in the city center. Officials discussed lowering electricity taxes, feeding surplus energy from electric vehicles back into national grids, and listened attentively when Ukrainian officials, invited alongside British, Norwegian and Moldovan delegates, offered to store European natural gas supplies on behalf of the bloc in its vast underground caverns, Moldova's energy minister, Dorin Junghietu, told POLITICO. Junghietu added that Europe needed "quick, tangible results" to bring down costs. He said the best way to do this was to make it easier and cheaper to invest in household renewables like solar, but acknowledged that this would be difficult in countries where deeper, structural changes to grids are necessary. The EU's helplessness was apparent when officials were pressed on whether the EU was prepared for a possible U.S. ban on fuel exports, after Trump appeared to endorse the idea earlier this month. Ministers largely expressed hope that such a ban wouldn't happen, while urging Washington to rethink. Jørgensen told reporters he sent a "clear signal" to his U.S. counterpart, Chris Wright, that the U.S. ought to retreat from the threat, and said he was happy to see Wright publicly agree that it wouldn't work. O'Brien said conversations with U.S. officials during a visit to Washington and New York last week had reassured him that the plan wouldn't go ahead. Advertisement Advertisement A third European energy official said there was "not much we can do ... in the short term in terms of oil prices," but that he hoped the ban wouldn't materialize. "The Americans are pragmatic people," the official said. "It’s all about the money — if they put a ban on diesel exports, it might work for Texas, but it wouldn't work for other parts of the U.S." On Tuesday, POLITICO reported that U.S. oil industry executives and White House officials were seeking alternatives to Trump's proposed diesel export ban. Options could include asking European governments to release diesel from their own strategic reserves, according to two people familiar with the discussions who were granted anonymity to discuss conversations with the White House. European officials acknowledged that it was ultimately in Trump's hands — and that there was little individual member countries could do to sway the U.S. president if it did go ahead. For "one particular member state, [it] will be extremely challenging to change a decision over the option," said Romanian state secretary for energy Cristian Busoi. "Trying to guess what Trump will do is like looking at a crystal ball," added the official cited above. That's not to say there are no options available for the EU. Fatih Birol, executive director of the International Energy Agency, a group of rich countries that coordinates energy policy, who was also present at the Dublin talks, acknowledged that Europe was "one of the most exposed regions." But he said that the IEA stood ready to coordinate the release of strategic petroleum stocks, while cautioning that such a move wasn't a priority — yet. "Our reserves are in good order," added O'Brien in a separate interview. "There’s no fear of an issue with regard to the depletion of reserves at this stage. What we do know is we have to plan for the worst and hope for the best."

https://www.rediff.com/news/interview/si.text: 'SIR Is Bloodless Political Genocide' '93 lakhs deletions in Bengal, 96 lakhs in Tamil Nadu, 24 lakhs in Kerala, 77 lakhs in Gujarat, 45 lakhs in Madhya Pradesh, 44 lakhs in Rajasthan. 2.89 crores in Uttar Pradesh.' Key Points 'SIR deletions could reach nearly 14 crore once the exercise is completed across remaining states.' 'Minorities, Dalits, Adivasis, migrants, labourers and poor women are disproportionately affected by voter deletions.' 'Voter deletion could affect future generations because subsequent SIR exercises may rely on previous voter mapping. 'Election Commission cannot determine citizenship and must refer doubtful cases to the competent authority.' 'Scrap SIR, restore the 2024 voter list and restructure the Election Commission with stronger safeguards.' Political economist Parakala Prabhakar has been a one-man army relentlessly fighting the working of the Election Commission of India, and the SIR process. In 2024 after the Lok Sabha elections, he told Rediff , 'All is not well with the Election Commission. They refused to be transparent and accountable.' In 2025, he told Rediff , 'This election commission has to go. It is the most partial. It functions more like a government department than an autonomous body.' In May 2026, questioning the SIR process, he told Rediff , 'SIR is nothing but bringing the NRC-CAA through backdoor. You are killing lakhs and lakhs of citizenships.' "When somebody is deleted from the voters list now, not only are they being deleted, but for generations to come, their progenies also will be deleted. Because the SIR exercise is based on 2000 P (2002/2003) voters list mapping," Mr Prabhakar tells Rediff 's Shobha Warrier in the concluding segment of a two-part must-read interview. Part I: 'Election Commission Is Shameless' You said in our last interview that they were killing lakhs and lakhs of citizenship. Yes, that's where I come to. Data has not come from Tripura and Nagaland. In Himachal, Ladakh, Jammu and Kashmir, the SIR process has not been started yet. Once these things are complete, I think the total figure of deletion is going to reach somewhere around 14 crores. 14 crore people is not a small number! 85% of the countries in this world have less than 14 crore population. What does it mean? It means that in India, this election campaign is killing and taking out a few countries and throwing them out. It amounts to that. 93 lakhs in Bengal, 96 lakhs in Tamil Nadu, 24 lakhs in Kerala, 77 lakhs in Gujarat, 45 lakhs in Madhya Pradesh, 44 lakhs in Rajasthan. 2.89 crores in Uttar Pradesh. Nearly 3 crores! It means the Yogi Adityanath government was elected by an electorate which consisted of 3 crore ineligible voters, right? Then, throw that government out. Now, you look at who are these people who are being taken out. It is not random as people thought earlier. It is very clear that a largely disproportionate number of people are Muslim minority, Christian minority, Dalits, Adivasis, marginalised people like daily wage labourers, migrant labourers, illiterate people who do not have documents, who cannot procure documents, poor people, and among all these sections, they are mostly women. These are the people who are targeted and being deleted. There is one more very serious implication. Now, when somebody is deleted from the voters list now, not only are they being deleted, but for generations to come, their progenies also will be deleted. Because the SIR exercise is based on 2000 P (2002/2003) voters list mapping. And future SIRs will be based on 2025-2026 mapping. So, if you are not a voter now, your progeny cannot be a voter later. So, by deleting one person today, you are deleting not only that person, but all the future generations of that individual. This is very serious. When people appeal against the deletion, there is a redressal. In Bengal, 28 lakh people are still waiting for appealing and adjudication, and without being adjudicated and declared, they were prevented from voting in the Bengal elections. When 28 lakh people were prevented from voting, how can such an election be a legitimate election? Now, the question is, is it being done to help a particular political party, and harm another political party? Most people, especially the media, the politicians, a lot of commentators are looking at what way is it helping the BJP, and in what way it is harming the INDIA bloc or the Congress? But my point is that for a couple of election cycles, this might help the BJP and harm the INDIA bloc. But there are longer term implications to what SIR is doing because it is targeting a particular section of society and taking them off the voter's list. It is clear they want to push some people out of the political society. Imagine 500 people living in a basti . None of them has vote. Would any political party go there? Would any candidate go there? Would any government give them roads, electricity, drinking water, health facility or a school? Nothing will be given because what they think about the government, about the legislator, doesn't matter to the legislator. They are no consequence. Which means that these people are out of the political society. The message is, if you want to live here without a franchise, without being taken care of, you live, otherwise get out. Like what the great chief minister of Assam said, I don't want these miya s, but I can't push them out. So, I'll create conditions in such a way that they themselves would leave. You said last time that SIR is nothing but bringing NRC-CAA through the backdoor... Exactly. SIR is CAA ( Citizens [Amendment] Act ) in disguise. It brings you to the fundamental question of who does this country belong to. When you are out of the electoral roll, you don't belong to this country, and the country doesn't belong to you. Is it the job of the Election Commission to prove the citizenship of a person? It is not. It's very clear in the Constitution. It is also very clear in the judgement of the Supreme Court of India delivered in May 2026 that while they can do SIR, they cannot decide on citizenship. In fact, it went to the extent of telling the Election Commission, if any of your officers found anybody's citizenship doubtful, it should make a list of them and refer to the competent authority under the citizenship act of 1955. They cannot on their own delete anybody. If the Election Commission's purpose is purportedly collecting SIR to weed out foreigners, let the Election Commission say that these many foreigners were found. They have not said a word about it so far. So, how do they justify this kind of industrial scale of deletion? As citizens, do the voters have to prove their identity to the Election Commission? Exactly. Since 1950 onwards, we always had this practice of including everyone within the border. Today you are not only excluding, but you are putting the burden of proving that you are eligible as the citizen. In any civilised society, jurisprudence is that if the State chooses somebody of something, the burden of proof lies with the state, and not with the individual. Next, a very cardinal principle of jurisprudence is that even if five culprits go free, not a single innocent person should be punished. Now, in the name of finding out some imaginary foreigner, you are depriving people of their citizenship, of their franchise. So, from any angle, this exercise is harming the roots of India's inclusive, secular, tolerant democracy. The core Constitutional values are under attack. I would term the SIR as a bloodless political genocide. Earlier in nation building in Africa, in America, in Europe, Yugoslavia, Hungary... everywhere, those who were not one of you were either pushed out of the borders or killed. In 2026, you can neither push out, nor can you kill. So, when you cannot exterminate a citizen, you exterminate his/her citizenship. Therefore, I call this bloodless political genocide. Earlier, there were bloody genocides, now it is bloodless political genocide. So, what should be done immediately? Should SIR be scrapped? SIR should be scrapped. We should go back to the 2024 voters list. And the body that is conducting SIR should be immediately disbanded. All the elections that have taken place on the basis of the SIR voters list should be annulled. A new Election Commission will have to be constituted on the basis of a completely, freshly redrawn rules, regulations and with enough checks and balances and proper guardrails. And the selection committee which has a majority for the executive should be changed. It should not only be properly balanced, but it should also be seen as properly balanced. Then withdraw the legislation that gave lifetime impunity to the Election Commission. These are the things that need to be done immediately.
